cultivar: Wuyuan local landrace with some Fuding Dabai
processing: Pan-fired then baked green: shoots are fired, rolled into a fine curve with the down raised, and dried gently, giving a slender eyebrow-shaped leaf.
harvest_season: Spring, from late March to late April; pre-Qingming and yu qian lots of a bud with one or two leaves.
appearance_dry: Slender, slightly curved, downy twists like eyebrows, deep green.
appearance_wet: Even bud-and-leaf sets, tender and bright green.
taste_profile: Sweet and thick with chestnut and orchid, a savoury middle and a long, clean sweetness.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass at 80–85 °C. A forgiving, sturdy green; four steeps is normal.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest in pre-Qingming and yu qian grades. Wuyuan is one of China's biggest exporters of certified organic green tea, so Ming Mei and plainer 'Wuyuan green' often carry organic certification; Ming Mei is the named premium style, the export grades are sold by number without a season. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Wuyuan Ming Mei is the premium green of Wuyuan county in north-eastern Jiangxi, historically part of the Huizhou tea country that also gave the world Keemun and Tunlü. Wuyuan green was a major export tea for a century, mostly as anonymous Chun Mee grades; Ming Mei, 'tea eyebrow', is the named, hand-finished style the county created in the late 1950s to show what its leaf could do.

It is made with a pan-firing followed by careful rolling into a slender curve and a gentle final drying that keeps the down, so the dry leaf looks like a finer, greener, fuzzier version of the eyebrow-shaped export tea it descends from.

In the cup it is sweet and quite thick: chestnut and orchid, a savoury middle and a long, clean sweetness, with more body than the Zhejiang bud teas and less roast than Anhui's. It is forgiving to brew, happy at 80–85 °C in a gaiwan, and good for four steeps. If a green from this region tastes smoky or sour, it is the export grade, not Ming Mei.

Wuyuan is one of China's largest sources of certified organic green tea, so Ming Mei and plain Wuyuan green frequently arrive with EU or US organic certificates, which is one reason the county's tea shows up in Western shops under generic names. Ming Mei proper is sold as the current year's spring tea in pre-Qingming and yu qian lots; the plainer tea is sold by export grade with no season. Look for slender, downy, even leaf and ask for the picking date.

Wuyuan in late March, when the rapeseed fields bloom around the whitewashed Huizhou-style villages, is one of the prettiest places in China to drink the new tea.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. Creation date 'late 1950s' follows Chinese sources (1958 is commonly cited).
